title: Question
text:
You call barplot() on a two-way contingency table without setting any additional arguments, and the resulting figure stacks each group’s bar on top of another. Which argument should you change to instead display the bars for each group side by side?



legend = TRUE
beside = TRUE
probability = TRUE
horiz = TRUE

title: Question
text:
legend = TRUE
beside = TRUE
probability = TRUE
horiz = TRUE

title: Question
text:
Answerlist

Wrong: legend only controls whether a legend is drawn; it does not change how the bars are arranged.
Correct: setting beside = TRUE places the bars for each group next to each other instead of stacking them.
Wrong: probability is a hist() argument for switching to a density scale, and has no effect on bar arrangement.
Wrong: horiz only flips the bars from vertical to horizontal; it doesn’t change stacking versus grouping.

title: Question
text:
You’ve already created a histogram and now want to add a kernel density curve on top of it, in the same figure. What happens if you call plot() on the density estimate to try to add it?



The density curve is drawn on top of the existing histogram, combining both into a single figure.
The plot() call opens a brand new figure, replacing the histogram instead of adding to it.
Nothing happens, since plot() cannot accept a density object as an argument.
R throws an error and stops execution.

title: Question
text:
The density curve is drawn on top of the existing histogram, combining both into a single figure.
The plot() call opens a brand new figure, replacing the histogram instead of adding to it.
Nothing happens, since plot() cannot accept a density object as an argument.
R throws an error and stops execution.

title: Question
text:
Answerlist

Wrong: plot() starts a new plot rather than drawing on top of an existing one.
Correct: plot() always draws a fresh figure; to add a layer to an existing plot, a dedicated layering function like lines() is needed instead.
Wrong: plot() can accept a density object; it just doesn’t layer it onto an existing figure.
Wrong: this doesn’t produce an error; it silently replaces the existing plot with a new one.

title: Knowledge Quiz: Bivariate Visualization
text:
Note




Click the check-mark button to check your answer.
Click the question-mark button to see an explanation of the solution.






You create a scatterplot of two variables and observe that the cloud of points trends downward from left to right: as the x-axis variable increases, the points tend to sit lower on the y-axis. What does this pattern suggest about the relationship between the two variables?

No association: the two variables are unrelated.A negative association: higher values of one variable tend to go with lower values of the other.A positive association: higher values of one variable tend to go with higher values of the other.A perfect, deterministic relationship: one variable can be predicted exactly from the other.




Wrong: a lack of association would show a shapeless cloud with no consistent up or down trend.
Correct: a downward-trending cloud indicates a negative (inverse) association between the two variables.
Wrong: a positive association would show the cloud trending upward, not downward.
Wrong: a trend alone doesn’t imply a perfect relationship; the points could still show substantial scatter around it.

Recall the conditional boxplot from the tutorial, created with boxplot(progress ~ sex, data = diabetes). Suppose that, instead of looking similar, the box for one sex group sat entirely above the box for the other, with little to no overlap between the two boxes. What would this suggest?

Sex would have no relationship with disease progression.The progress variable would not have been measured correctly for one of the two groups.That sex group would tend to have meaningfully higher disease progression than the other.The two sex groups would have identical disease progression distributions.




Wrong: a lack of relationship would show similarly positioned, overlapping boxes for both groups.

title: Question
text:
Why is a bar plot, rather than a histogram, the appropriate choice for visualizing the distribution of a categorical variable such as ticket class?



Because bar plots can only display continuous, numeric data.
Because a categorical variable has distinct, unordered or ordered levels, not a continuous range that needs to be divided into bins.
Because histograms cannot display counts, only proportions.
Because bar plots and histograms are interchangeable, so either one works equally well for any variable.

title: Question
text:
Because bar plots can only display continuous, numeric data.
Because a categorical variable has distinct, unordered or ordered levels, not a continuous range that needs to be divided into bins.
Because histograms cannot display counts, only proportions.
Because bar plots and histograms are interchangeable, so either one works equally well for any variable.

title: Question
text:
Answerlist

Wrong: bar plots are specifically meant for categorical, not continuous, data.
Correct: bar plots represent counts per category, with gaps between bars to show that categories are distinct, rather than binning a continuous range.
Wrong: histograms can display raw counts by default, and can be converted to proportions with the probability argument.
Wrong: using the wrong plot type misrepresents the nature of the variable (continuous vs. categorical).

title: Question
text:
Suppose you have a large sample from a smooth, roughly normal variable. If you increase the number of bins in a histogram of this variable from a small number (e.g., 5) to a very large number (e.g., 200), what generally happens to the histogram’s appearance?



It becomes progressively smoother, revealing an increasingly clear and simple shape.
It becomes more jagged, with bin-to-bin fluctuations caused by having only a few observations per bin.
Its shape reverses, so a right-skewed distribution appears left-skewed.
Its appearance stays exactly the same, since only bin width changes, not the underlying data.

title: Question
text:
It becomes progressively smoother, revealing an increasingly clear and simple shape.
It becomes more jagged, with bin-to-bin fluctuations caused by having only a few observations per bin.
Its shape reverses, so a right-skewed distribution appears left-skewed.
Its appearance stays exactly the same, since only bin width changes, not the underlying data.

title: Question
text:
Answerlist

Wrong: more bins means fewer observations per bin, which introduces more random noise, not less.
Correct: with very many bins, each bin contains very few observations, so bar heights become noisy and jagged.
Wrong: increasing the number of bins does not change which side of the distribution has the longer tail.
Wrong: the number of bins directly changes how the data are grouped, so the plot’s appearance does change.

title: Scatterplots
text:
Scatterplots are one of the most fundamental tools for visualizing the relationship between two continuous variables (or variables that we wish to treat as continuous). Each point on the plot represents one observational unit’s values on the two plotted variables. This makes scatterplots particularly useful for identifying trends, clusters, and extreme values in the data.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Do: We make a simple scatterplot with the plot() function. For example, the following code uses the diabetes dataset to visualize the bivariate association between Body Mass Index, bmi, and Total Cholesterol, tc. Higher body fat is generally linked to less favorable cholesterol levels in the clinical literature.

plot(y = diabetes$tc, x = diabetes$bmi)








See: every point represents a different patient’s value of BMI and their level of total cholesterol. The points form a cloud with a slight upward trend, suggesting that higher BMI values tend to be associated with higher cholesterol levels, although the variability is substantial.
We can improve the readability by adding axis labels, a title, and adjusting the axis limits. To do so we adjust the following parameters.

ylab, xlab: Define new axis labels
main: Add a plot title
ylim, xlim: Define the ranges of the y-axis and x-axis

Predict: these arguments only change the plot’s cosmetics; before running the code, predict whether the underlying pattern of points (their positions relative to each other) will change at all.

plot(y = diabetes$tc,
     x = diabetes$bmi,
     ylab = "Total Cholesterol",
     xlab = "Body Mass Index",
     main = "Relation between BMI and Cholesterol",
     ylim = c(0, 350),
     xlim = c(0, 50))








Explain: as predicted, the points themselves sit in exactly the same relative positions as before; only the labels, title, and the visible range of each axis have changed, making the figure easier to read without altering the underlying data.
When we apply plot() to a data frame containing only numeric columns, we generate a scatterplot matrix: a grid of scatterplots showing all the pairwise relationships. Do: Run the code below that selects 5 numeric columns.

plot(diabetes[c("age", "bmi", "tc", "glu", "progress")])








See: The grid contains 5 × 5 = 25 panels, one for every pair of the 5 selected variables (including each variable plotted against itself along the diagonal). Reading across a row or down a column lets us compare one variable’s relationship with every other variable at a glance, without having to build each scatterplot individually.






Practice Exercise

The diabetes dataset is already loaded in the working directory of this webr session.

title: Bivariate Visualizations
text:
In the second part of this module, we will cover visualizations that allow us to scrutinize the bivariate distribution of two variables.
Such bivariate visualizations allow us to inspect the nature of the association between two numeric variables, for example, or how the distribution of a numeric variable differs between groups. Hence, bivariate visualizations are very useful for exploratory data analysis and diagnosing issues in statistical models like linear regression.

title: Univariate Visualizations
text:
We will begin this module by exploring some of the main univariate visualizations that we can create using Base R graphics.
One of the primary reasons we use data visualization is to scrutinize the univariate distributions of individual variables in our data. For example, we may want to check how closely some variables follow a normal distribution, or we might want to screen for extreme values. Univariate visualizations are ideally suited to these types of analysis.
We will cover histograms and kernel density plots for visualizing the distribution of numeric variables, boxplots for summarizing distributions and flagging potential outliers, and bar plots for visualizing the distribution of categorical variables.



 Back to top

title: Kernel Density Plots
text:
Density plots and their Bandwidth
A kernel density plot provides a smoothed estimate of a continuous variable’s distribution. You can think of a density plot as a smoothed version of a histogram: instead of counting observations into discrete bins, a density plot draws a continuous curve that estimates how the probability mass is distributed across the range of the variable. Because they don’t rely on bins, density plots are especially useful for comparing the distributions of several groups on the same chart without the visual clutter of overlapping bars.
In Base R, there isn’t a single function that both computes and plots a kernel density estimate in one step. Instead, we first compute a density estimate with the density() function, and then we plot the resulting object.
Do: Run the code below

d <- density(diabetes$bmi)
plot(d)








See: The code visualizes the distribution of BMI in the diabetes dataset. Given that BMI in a general patient population tends to have a long tail toward higher values, the curve is right-skewed. It mirrors the same kind of asymmetry we saw in the BMI histogram, only now represented as a single smooth line instead of a series of bars.
Just as a histogram’s appearance depends on its bin width, a density plot’s smoothness depends on its bandwidth: a parameter that controls how much the estimate smooths out the underlying data. We can control the bandwidth via the bw argument to density().
Predict: What will happen to the curve as we move from a very small bandwidth to a very large one. Will the curve become smoother or spikier as the bandwidth increases?
Explain:

plot(density(diabetes$bmi, bw = 0.3),
     main = "Very Small Bandwidth")







plot(density(diabetes$bmi, bw = 5),
     main = "Very Large Bandwidth")








When running the code above, you see that with a very small bandwidth, the curve closely tracks every small fluctuation in the data, producing a spiky, under-smoothed estimate that mostly reflects sampling noise rather than the true shape of the distribution. With a very large bandwidth, the curve becomes very smooth, but an overly large bandwidth can smooth away real features of the distribution, such as separate modes or a sharp peak. As with histogram bin width, choosing a reasonable bandwidth is a balance between showing genuine structure and swamping the plot with noise.






Common Mistake



It’s tempting to trust whatever bandwidth density() chooses by default and read the resulting curve at face value. But the default bandwidth is just one reasonable choice among many, and a curve that looks perfectly smooth might be hiding real structure in the data (oversmoothing), while a jagged curve might be mostly noise (undersmoothing). It’s good practice to try a couple of different bandwidth values, as we did above, before drawing conclusions about the shape of a distribution from a density plot alone.

title: Basic Visualization
text:
Welcome to the module on basic data visualization in R. Graphical visualizations are a crucial tool in data analysis because they allow us to explore, summarize, and communicate patterns in data that would be difficult to detect through numbers alone. Well-chosen visualizations can reveal trends, clusters, correlations, and outliers at a glance, helping to guide further analysis and support clear, persuasive communication of results.
In this module, we will explore the main plotting capabilities built into base R, focusing on five foundational types of visualization: histograms, kernel density plots, boxplots, bar plots, and scatterplots. Each section combines conceptual explanation with hands-on examples to show how to create and customize these plots in R, highlighting how they can be adapted to different datasets and analysis goals.

title: Basic Visualization
text:
Base R Graphics
R includes a versatile set of built-in plotting tools that allow us to create a wide range of visualizations without the need for additional packages. With these Base R plotting functions you can produce anything from simple scatterplots and histograms to more elaborate multi-panel displays.
Plots in Base R are built up step-by-step. You begin with a main plotting function such as plot(), hist(), or boxplot(), and then refine the result by adding or adjusting titles, axis labels, colors, and other visual elements. This way of working makes Base R graphics particularly useful for exploratory analysis, where it is often important to obtain quick visual feedback.
Although more advanced plotting packages like ggplot2 offer a more structured, layered approach, Base R graphics remain useful for rapidly inspecting datasets and creating lightweight graphics without extra dependencies.

title: Basic Visualization
text:
Learning Goals
After completing this module, you will be able to use Base R functions to create:

Histograms to visualize the distributions of numeric variables
Kernel density plots to visualize smoothed distributions of numeric variables
Boxplots to summarize distributions, detect outliers, and compare groups
Bar plots to visualize the distributions of categorical variables
Scatterplots to investigate relationships between two numeric variables

You will also learn how to create conditional plots and how to add information to your visualizations by drawing extra layers on existing plots.
Click the button below to get started with the first tutorial.


 Begin Tutorial

title: Conclusion
text: By completing this module, you’ve taken your first steps toward data visualization with R. You’ve learned how to use Base R graphics to create some of the most useful types of data visualization: histograms, kernel density plots, boxplots, bar plots, and scatterplots. You also learned how to convert univariate plots into conditional plots and how to add layers to plots to increase the information provided by a single figure.

title: Histograms
text:
Histograms are one of the most straightforward and useful ways to visualize the distribution of a numeric variable. A histogram shows the distribution of a single numeric variable by dividing its range into bins (intervals), counting how many observations fall into each bin, and visualizing these counts as bars in a plot. Histograms are meant to represent a variable’s probability distribution, so they’re useful for understanding the shape, spread, and skewness of numeric variables.
The hist() function in Base R creates histograms.
Do: Run the code below.

hist(diabetes$glu)








See: The code visualizes the distribution of blood glucose levels in the diabetes dataset. Blood glucose measurements in a general patient population tend to cluster around a normal range, with a smaller number of patients showing elevated readings. You can see that this distribution is right-skwed: most glucose readings cluster at the lower end of the range, with a longer tail stretching toward higher, less common values.
By default, hist() will try to best represent the distribution by applying the Sturges Formula to define the bin width. We can alter this behavior in several ways through the breaks argument.

Specify a different built-in algorithm
Provide a vector of cut points giving the bin margins
Request a fixed number of bins
Define our own function to create the bins

Predict: What will happen to the histogram of blood glucose as we go from very few bins (5) to very many bins (50). Will the distribution’s shape become clearer or noisier?

hist(diabetes$glu,
     main = "Define bins via Scott's formula",
     breaks = "scott")







hist(diabetes$glu,
     main = "Define bins with a vector",
     breaks = seq(50, 130, 10))







hist(diabetes$glu, main = "Ask for 5 bins", breaks = 5)







hist(diabetes$glu, main = "Ask for 50 bins", breaks = 50)








Explain: With only 5 bins, the histogram is coarse: it still shows the right skew, but hides finer details about where exactly the data cluster. With 50 bins, individual bars become sparse and jagged, since each bin now contains only a handful of observations, and this bin-to-bin noise can look like “real” bumps in the distribution that aren’t actually meaningful. Choosing a sensible number of bins is therefore a balance between hiding structure (too few bins) and amplifying random noise (too many bins).

title: Histograms
text:
Customizing the plot
Do: You can customize the appearance of the plot in many ways, using the many parameters that the hist() function accepts. Some examples of parameters that can be adjusted are:

main: Add a better title
col: Change the fill color of the bars
border: Change the border color of the bars
probability: Switch the y-axis to a probability scale

See: By running the code below and comparing the new plot to the previous one, you can see how the changes are implemented in practice:

hist(diabetes$glu,
     main = "Colorful Histogram",
     col = "pink",
     border = "blue",
     probability = FALSE)








Predict: How will the y-axis change once we set probability = TRUE instead of leaving it at its default. Will the bars themselves change shape, or just what the y-axis represents?

hist(diabetes$glu,
     main = "Colorful Histogram",
     col = "pink",
     border = "blue",
     probability = TRUE)








Explain: As you can see, the bars are exactly the same shape as before, only the y-axis has changed. Setting probability = TRUE converts the y-axis to a probability scale and makes the histogram’s total area sum to 1. Hence the bar heights represent the proportion of the sample that falls into each bin, rather than a straight count of the observations in each bin.

Graphical Parameters

title: Bar Plots
text:
Bar plots are the analogue of histograms for discrete variables. Whereas the columns in a histogram are defined by counting the number of cases that fall into arbitrary bins, the bars in a bar plots represent the number of cases that belong to each level of a categorical variable.
We use the barplot() function to create bar plots in Base R. As with kernel density plots, however, we first need to summarize the data before creating the visualization. Specifically, we use the table() function to create a frequency table, and we then plot that table with barplot().
Do: Run the following code that visualizes the distribution of ticket classes in the titanic dataset. On a ship like the Titanic, third class tickets were generally the cheapest and most numerous. Before running the code, think about which ticket class you’d expect to have the tallest bar.

# Tabulate the counts of each ticket class
classTable <- table(titanic$class)

# Create a bar plot to visualize the frequency of ticket classes
barplot(classTable)








See: In the plot we see that the third class has the tallest bar by a wide margin, reflecting that most passengers travelled in the cheapest ticket class.
Predict: To plot the counts as proportions, we convert the data in the table before plotting. Predict how this will change the bar plot: will the bars change height relative to each other, or just the numbers shown on the y-axis?

# Convert counts to proportions
classProps <- classTable / sum(classTable)

# Create a bar plot to visualize the frequency of ticket classes
barplot(classProps)








Explain: As with the switch from counts to a probability scale in a histogram, the bars keep exactly the same relative heights; only the y-axis has changed, now showing the proportion of passengers in each class instead of the raw count.
As with all of our Base R plotting, we can tweak the appearance in many ways. For example, setting horiz = TRUE flips the orientation of the bars. Which axis will now show the ticket classes, and which will show the counts?

barplot(classTable,
        horiz = TRUE,
        main = "Classes of Titanic Tickets",
        ylab = "Ticket Class",
        xlab = "Number of Passengers",
        col = rgb(181, 137, 0, max = 255),
        border = rgb(0, 43, 54, max = 255))








The ticket classes now run along the y-axis, and the bars extend horizontally to show the passenger counts along the x-axis; the underlying data haven’t changed, only the layout of the plot.






Common Mistake



Bar plots and histograms can look similar at a glance, but they visualize different kinds of variables. A bar plot’s bars are separated by gaps because each bar represents a distinct, unordered or ordered category (e.g., a ticket class); there’s no meaningful “in-between” value connecting one bar to the next. A histogram’s bars touch because they represent contiguous bins across a continuous range, where every value in between is meaningful. Using a bar plot for a continuous numeric variable (or a histogram for a categorical one) misrepresents the nature of the data.

title: Boxplots
text:
The boxplot (AKA, box-and-whiskers plot) is one of the most enduring contributions of Tukey’s seminal book Exploratory Data Analysis. A boxplot is a visualization of a numeric variable’s so-call “five-number-summary” that quantifies a variable’s distribution through five order statistics: minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, maximum. Boxplots are particularly useful for evaluating the spread and symmetry of a distribution and checking for extreme values.
Do: Run the code below that uses the boxplot() function to create a boxplot with Base R graphics of BMI from the diabetes dataset.

boxplot(diabetes$bmi)








See: Similar to what we saw with the histogram and density plot, BMI has a long right tail. In a boxplot, we see that as the median falls closer to first quartile than the third quartile, and the upper whisker is longer than the lower whisker.
The “box” part of a box-and-whiskers plot is always defined by first and third quartiles, \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\), with the median drawn somewhere inside the box. So, this box tells us something about the symmetry and spread of the middle 50% of the distribution.
The “whiskers”, on the other hand, tell us about the tails of the distribution. We can define the whiskers in several different ways to target specific information. In the default boxplot, the whiskers are defined in terms of the inner-quartile range \(\textrm{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\).

Lower whisker: \(Q_1 - 1.5 \times \textrm{IQR}\)
Upper whisker: \(Q_3 + 1.5 \times \textrm{IQR}\)

We can change the weight applied to the IQR via the range argument.
Predict: What will happen to the number of points plotted as individual outliers if we widen the whisker margin from \(1.5 \times
\textrm{IQR}\) to \(2 \times \textrm{IQR}\): will more or fewer points fall outside the whiskers?

boxplot(diabetes$bmi,
        range = 2,
        xlab = "Body Mass Index",
        main = "Margin = 3 * IQR")








Explain: Widening the margin pulls the whiskers further out, so fewer points fall outside them and get flagged as individual outliers. Taking this to its logical extreme, we can set range = 0 to use the minimum and maximum values to define the whiskers, meaning no observations get flagged as outliers at all.

boxplot(diabetes$bmi,
        range = 0,
        xlab = "Body Mass Index",
        main = "Min/Max Whiskers")










Any observations that fall outside the interval defined by the whiskers are plotted as individual points. This behavior makes boxplots a handy way to check for extreme values (i.e., outliers). If we set the whiskers so they define the range of plausible values, any points that fall outside the whiskers are possible outliers.
A common convention is to use a margin of \(1.5 \times \textrm{IQR}\) to flag “possible” outliers and a margin of \(3
\times \textrm{IQR}\) to flag “probable” outliers.
Do: Run the code below to use the \(1.5 \times \textrm{IQR}\) for flagging possible outliers.

boxplot(diabetes$bmi,
        range = 1.5,
        xlab = "Body Mass Index",
        main = "Possible Outliers")








See: With the default \(1.5 \times \textrm{IQR}\) margin, several observations fall outside the whiskers and are plotted as individual points flagged as possible outliers.
Predict: Before looking at a boxplot with a wider margin, predict what will happen to the number of flagged points if we widen the whisker margin to \(3 \times \textrm{IQR}\): will more or fewer points be flagged as outliers?

boxplot(diabetes$bmi,
        range = 3,
        xlab = "Body Mass Index",
        main = "Probable Outliers")








Explain: Widening the margin to \(3 \times \textrm{IQR}\) pulls the whiskers further out, so fewer points fall outside them: 3 observations are flagged as possible outliers, compared to only 0 flagged as probable outliers under the wider margin.






Common Mistake



It’s tempting to treat every point flagged by the default \(1.5 \times \textrm{IQR}\) rule as a genuine data error that should be removed. But this rule is just a heuristic convention, not a statistical test for whether an observation is “real” or not. A flagged point might be a legitimate, if unusual, observation. Before removing or downweighting any flagged points, it’s worth checking whether they make substantive sense given what you know about the variable.

title: Boxplots
text:
The boxplot (AKA, box-and-whiskers plot) is one of the most enduring contributions of Tukey’s seminal book Exploratory Data Analysis. A boxplot is a visualization of a numeric variable’s so-call “five-number-summary” that quantifies a variable’s distribution through five order statistics: minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, maximum. Boxplots are particularly useful for evaluating the spread and symmetry of a distribution and checking for extreme values.
Do: Run the code below that uses the boxplot() function to create a boxplot with Base R graphics of BMI from the diabetes dataset.

boxplot(diabetes$bmi)








See: Similar to what we saw with the histogram and density plot, BMI has a long right tail. In a boxplot, we see that as the median falls closer to first quartile than the third quartile, and the upper whisker is longer than the lower whisker.
The “box” part of a box-and-whiskers plot is always defined by first and third quartiles, \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\), with the median drawn somewhere inside the box. So, this box tells us something about the symmetry and spread of the middle 50% of the distribution.

title: Conditional & Combined Plots
text:
We can convert most univariate visualizations that we create with Base R graphics into conditional plots by specifying a grouping factor. We then get a single figure with group-specific versions of the univariate visualization.

Boxplots
We can use conditional boxplots to compare the distribution of a variable across groups. To create this type of figure, we employ the so-called formula interface when calling the boxplot() function.
Do: Run the following code to create sex-specific boxplots of disease progression using the diabetes dataset. Would you expect disease progression to differ noticeably between the two sex groups, or to look fairly similar?

boxplot(progress ~ sex, data = diabetes)








See: The two boxplots look broadly similar in level and spread, suggesting disease progression doesn’t differ dramatically between the sexes in this sample. When we use the formula interface, we define the plot’s structure through an R formula object that we specify as the first argument to boxplot(). In this formula, progress ~ sex, we specify the plotted variable on the left-hand side of the formula and we put the grouping factor on the right-hand side of the formula. We also have to use the data argument to specify a data frame where boxplot() can find the variables we’re referencing in the formula.

Practice Exercise



Use the titanic dataset to create a conditional boxplot to visualize the distributions of age within the groups defined by the survived variable.

What does this figure tell you about the ages of survivors (survived = 'yes') vs. non-survivors (survived = 'no')?

NOTE: The titanic dataset is already loaded into the working directory of this webr session.

 Interactive Editor Solution



Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.



boxplot(age ~ survived, data = titanic)








The median age does not seem to differ much between the two groups, but the survivors’ distribution appears to be more symmetric, and there are fewer old survivors. The non-survivors’ distribution is positively skewed by the disproportionately higher number of fatalities among older passengers.







Bar Plots
Conditional bar plots visualize two dimensional contingency tables. So, these types of figure allow us to evaluate how the distribution of one categorical variable differs across levels of some other variable.
To create a conditional bar plot, we fist create a two-way contingency table, and then we plot that table with the barplot() function.
Do: Run the following code that uses the titanic dataset to visualize the conditional distributions of ticket classes for the two survival groups. What will barplot() do by default with a two-way table: will it place the bars for each survival group side by side, or stack them on top of each other?

# Cross-tabulate ticket class and survival status
tab <- table(titanic$class, titanic$survived)

# Visualize the table created above
barplot(tab)








See: by default, barplot() stacks the bars for each ticket class group on top of each other. This default choice creates two important problems.

The bars for each ticket class group are stacked, so the meaning of the values shown on the y-axis is ambiguous
We don’t know which ticket group is represented by which color.

Predict: How can we adjust the plot to solve these problems?

# Create a better visualization of the table
barplot(tab, beside = TRUE, legend = TRUE)








Explain: We can solve these problems by plotting the bars beside each other by setting beside = TRUE and drawing a legend by setting legend = TRUE.
Now, we have a useful visualization. From this figure, we can clearly see that the relative survival rates of passengers traveling in third class were much worse than the survival rates of other passengers.

barplot(tab, 
        beside = TRUE, 
        legend = TRUE,
        xlab = "Survived",
        main = "Survival Status of Titanic Passengers by Gender")








The relative survival rates are much better for female passengers. The number of males in the survived = 'no' group is much higher than the number of females, and the patterns is reversed in the survived = 'yes' group.







Histograms
When generating histograms, we can’t really create the same kind of conditional plots that we can with boxplots and bar plots, but we can overlay different plot layers to add useful information to our figure.
Do: Run the following code to draw a kernel density plot on top of an existing histogram.

# Create a basic histogram of blood glucose levels
hist(diabetes$glu, probability = TRUE)

# Calculate the kernel density estimate of blood glucose levels
d <- density(diabetes$glu)

# Overlay the kernel density curve on the histogram
lines(y = d$y, x = d$x, col = "red")








See: The red curve is added on top of the existing histogram, it does not replace it. This works because lines() is a layering function: it draws on top of whatever plot is already open, rather than starting a new one. Note that we’re explicitly extracting the x and y vectors from the object returned by density() to define the x and y coordinates of the line.
The Base R graphical suite offers many functions like lines() that add layers to existing plots.
Predict: What is the function of the lines added by the code below?

# Create a basic histogram of average blood pressure levels
hist(diabetes$bp)

# Calculate the boundaries of the central interval containing 90% of observations
ci <- quantile(diabetes$bp, prob = c(0.025, 0.975))

# Add dashed lines to denoting the upper and lower 5% tail area cutoffs
abline(v = ci, lty = 2, lwd = 2)








Explain: The abline() adds two dashed lines to denote the boundaries of the region containing the central 90% of observations.






Common Mistake



It’s tempting to reach for plot() (or hist(), boxplot(), etc.) whenever you want to add something to a figure. But these are all functions that draw a brand new plot, replacing whatever was there before, rather than adding to it. To add a layer to an existing plot, you need a dedicated layering function instead, such as lines(), points(), or abline(). If your intended overlay disappears and the plot looks unchanged (or a new plot appears in its place), check whether you accidentally used a plotting function instead of a layering one.




Scatterplots
We can apply the same type of layering process to mark up scatterplots with additional information.
Do: Run the code below to add the least squares best fit line to a scatterplot showing the relation between average blood pressure, bp, and blood glucose levels, glu.

# Create a scatterplot of blood pressure against blood glucose
plot(bp ~ glu, data = diabetes, pch = 19)

# Estimate the linear regression of blood pressure on blood glucose
lmOut <- lm(bp ~ glu, data = diabetes)

# Add the best fit line to the scatterplot
abline(reg = lmOut, lwd = 2, col = "blue")








See: The fitted line slopes upward, indicating that higher blood glucose levels tend to go along with higher average blood pressure. Again, we use the abline() function to overlay a line onto the existing plot. In this case, however, we define the line based on the estimated regression coefficients stored in the lmOut object that we created with the lm() function.

title: Knowledge Quiz: Univariate Visualizations
text:
Note




Click the check-mark button to check your answer.
Click the question-mark button to see an explanation of the solution.






Suppose you have a large sample from a smooth, roughly normal variable. If you increase the number of bins in a histogram of this variable from a small number (e.g., 5) to a very large number (e.g., 200), what generally happens to the histogram’s appearance?

Its shape reverses, so a right-skewed distribution appears left-skewed.Its appearance stays exactly the same, since only bin width changes, not the underlying data.It becomes progressively smoother, revealing an increasingly clear and simple shape.It becomes more jagged, with bin-to-bin fluctuations caused by having only a few observations per bin.




Wrong: increasing the number of bins does not change which side of the distribution has the longer tail.
Wrong: the number of bins directly changes how the data are grouped, so the plot’s appearance does change.
Wrong: more bins means fewer observations per bin, which introduces more random noise, not less.
Correct: with very many bins, each bin contains very few observations, so bar heights become noisy and jagged.





You want to compare the distributions of a numeric variable across three groups on the same plot. Why might overlaid kernel density plots be preferable to overlaid histograms for this purpose?

Because density plots ignore differences in sample size between the groups being compared.Because density plots don’t require choosing any smoothing parameter, unlike histograms, which require choosing bins.Because density plots draw smooth, continuous curves that can be overlaid without the visual clutter of overlapping bars.Because density plots always reveal more detail about the data than histograms do.




Wrong: density plots are still affected by sample size, just like histograms.
Wrong: density plots still require choosing a smoothing parameter, the bandwidth, which plays a role similar to bin width.
Correct: continuous curves are easier to visually separate and compare than several sets of overlapping bars.
Wrong: whether a density plot reveals more or less detail depends on the chosen bandwidth, just as a histogram depends on bin choice.





In a boxplot, the median line sits much closer to \(Q_1\) than to \(Q_3\), and the upper whisker is noticeably longer than the lower whisker. What does this suggest about the underlying distribution?

The distribution is roughly symmetric.The distribution is right-skewed (positively skewed), with a longer tail toward higher values.The distribution has no variability.The distribution is left-skewed (negatively skewed), with a longer tail toward lower values.




Wrong: a symmetric distribution would have the median roughly centered in the box, with whiskers of similar length.
Correct: a median pulled toward \(Q_1\) combined with a longer upper whisker is the signature of a right-skewed distribution.
Wrong: a distribution with no variability would show a box collapsed to a single line, not this pattern.
Wrong: this pattern would instead show the median pulled toward \(Q_3\) with a longer lower whisker.





Why is a bar plot, rather than a histogram, the appropriate choice for visualizing the distribution of a categorical variable such as ticket class?

Because bar plots and histograms are interchangeable, so either one works equally well for any variable.Because bar plots can only display continuous, numeric data.Because histograms cannot display counts, only proportions.Because a categorical variable has distinct, unordered or ordered levels, not a continuous range that needs to be divided into bins.




Wrong: using the wrong plot type misrepresents the nature of the variable (continuous vs. categorical).
Wrong: bar plots are specifically meant for categorical, not continuous, data.
Wrong: histograms can display raw counts by default, and can be converted to proportions with the probability argument.
Correct: bar plots represent counts per category, with gaps between bars to show that categories are distinct, rather than binning a continuous range.

title: Question
text:
You create a scatterplot of two variables and observe that the cloud of points trends downward from left to right: as the x-axis variable increases, the points tend to sit lower on the y-axis. What does this pattern suggest about the relationship between the two variables?



A positive association: higher values of one variable tend to go with higher values of the other.
A negative association: higher values of one variable tend to go with lower values of the other.
No association: the two variables are unrelated.
A perfect, deterministic relationship: one variable can be predicted exactly from the other.

title: Question
text:
A positive association: higher values of one variable tend to go with higher values of the other.
A negative association: higher values of one variable tend to go with lower values of the other.
No association: the two variables are unrelated.
A perfect, deterministic relationship: one variable can be predicted exactly from the other.

title: Question
text:
Answerlist

Wrong: a positive association would show the cloud trending upward, not downward.
Correct: a downward-trending cloud indicates a negative (inverse) association between the two variables.
Wrong: a lack of association would show a shapeless cloud with no consistent up or down trend.
Wrong: a trend alone doesn’t imply a perfect relationship; the points could still show substantial scatter around it.

Recall the conditional boxplot from the tutorial, created with boxplot(progress ~ sex, data = diabetes). Suppose that, instead of looking similar, the box for one sex group sat entirely above the box for the other, with little to no overlap between the two boxes. What would this suggest?



That sex group would tend to have meaningfully higher disease progression than the other.
The two sex groups would have identical disease progression distributions.
Sex would have no relationship with disease progression.
The progress variable would not have been measured correctly for one of the two groups.
